title: Burst throttle and KV ticketing protocol for graceful OOM circumvention
creator: Sofia Patel
description:
Problem: Production clusters occasionally hit transient GPU OOMs during sudden traffic bursts that force aggressive KV eviction and break streaming requests. Existing fallback paths trigger coarse model downshifts or full request retries, causing tail latency spikes and degraded response quality.

Goal: Implement a lightweight, per-request 'ticketing' mechanism that serializes KV/working-set admission under short-lived burst pressure, plus a burst-throttle flow that gracefully degrades token fidelity and retries at controlled intervals. The mechanism should avoid full model fallback unless sustained pressure persists, minimize tail latency regression, and keep cost impact bounded.

Key constraints: must be deployable without changing user API, operate at request-admission level (not per-token policy), interoperate with continuous batching, and respect dedicated-customer isolation (no cross-tenant eviction). Must preserve streaming semantics where possible and be reversible (fast restore of fidelity).
acceptance_criteria:
1) Under synthetic burst test (3x baseline RPS for 60s) cluster OOM rate remains <0.5% and successful graceful degradations occur instead of hard failures.
2) Mean 95p latency increase attributable to the protocol <= 10% compared to baseline.
3) No user-visible content-quality regression for steady-state traffic (A/B with control).
4) Feature is toggleable per-deployment and has an SLO-based kill switch.
5) End-to-end e2e test + load test in CI and perf dashboards added.
rollout_plan:
Phase 1: deploy to internal staging (runtime-1.21) behind feature flag, run 48h soak with synthetic burst generator and real workloads (canary 5%).
Phase 2: increment to 25% production traffic on non-enterprise pools for 72h with close monitoring.
Phase 3: enable on dedicated pools with opt-in per-customer; collect telemetry for 2 weeks before wider default.
Fallback: feature flag and SLO-based automated rollback (via console-ops).
test_plan: Unit tests for ticket lifecycle, integration tests for admission under concurrent batching, chaos test that kills a GPU mid-burst to validate graceful degrade+restore, and load tests with variable KV hit-rate to measure eviction reduction. Add golden prompt set run to detect quality regressions. CI job: runtime/ticketing-smoke and perf/load/gpu-burst.
implementation_notes:
Design summary: introduce a lightweight 'KV Ticket' object tracked in the admission service (in-memory, sharded per-GPU pool). Tickets are short-lived leases (~500ms) that gate the ability to claim additional KV working set or join large continuous-batches. When tickets are scarce we apply a graded degradation: 1) prefix trimming of low-priority tokens, 2) temporary small-quantized path for tail requests, 3) model variant downshift only for requests that explicitly opt into safety fallback.

Admission algorithm: token-window estimate -> ticket request -> if ticket denied: fast-path degrade or queue up to 150ms. Ticket release on batch completion. Tickets are budgeted per-GPU and weighted by request priority. Metrics: ticket_wait_ms, ticket_denied_rate, degraded_request_rate, kv_eviction_rate, oom_count.

Trade-offs: small increase in admission latency for some requests vs. large reduction in hard OOMs. We avoid cross-tenant eviction by scoping ticket pools; this can reduce overall utilization during bursts for fairness. Implementation avoids global coordination (local to pool) to keep latency low.
